title: The rest of the poem
hook: the full poem survives in Tibetan and Chinese, carrying the story to the relics

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahakassapa comes, and your line: the great ones arrive. Did you thank someone who came later than you? Today, the end of the week, and the end of the poem's road. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

A book with its last chapters torn out, and a friend overseas who happens to own a copy. That's roughly the situation with this poem. The Sanskrit text, the language Ashvaghosha wrote in, breaks off partway through the story. If that were all there was, the life in verse would stop in the middle of the night under the tree, before the dawn. But the poem was carried abroad and translated, into Tibetan and into Chinese. And in those versions, the story keeps going, all the way to the end.
screen: `A BOOK WITH ITS LAST PAGES GONE.` → `THE SANSKRIT BREAKS OFF.` → `TIBETAN AND CHINESE CARRY ON.`

segments.voice: So what's in the rest of the poem? Four stretches. First, the gifts of land. A rich merchant, Anathapindika, buys a prince's grove for the Buddha and the monks, so they have a place to stay through the rains. The teaching has a home. Second, the return. The Buddha goes back to his father's city, the one he left through the silent gates. The king who tried to keep him in meets a son who comes back as a teacher, and listens. Third, the trouble and the welcome. A cousin, Devadatta, turns against him and sets a maddened elephant loose in his path, and the elephant stops and grows calm before him. And a courtesan, Amrapali, welcomes him into her mango grove and gives it to the community. The poem honors her gift. Fourth, the end. The Buddha, old and ill, makes his last journey, lies down between two sala trees at Kushinagara, gives his last teaching, and passes into final nirvana. And near its close the poem goes one step further than the death: the kings of the region quarrel over his relics, nearly go to war, and then agree to share them, each carrying a portion home to honor. So the story closes with the life scattered across many places, and kept. And notice the echo. The poem itself had the same fate. Scattered, carried, kept in other languages. Look back at this week: Mara came with a bow of flowers; Mara was defeated; the night of knowing; dharmacakra; many came; Mahakassapa came. And now the rest of the poem, carried home by other hands.
screen: `A GROVE FOR THE RAINS.` · `HOME TO HIS FATHER'S CITY.` · `AN ELEPHANT, A MANGO GROVE.` · `THE SALA TREES, AND THE RELICS SHARED.` · then, large: `THE POEM TRAVELED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up where the poem traveled. After the sit, if you're curious, open a map and trace the roads a book could take from northern India, north to Tibet, and by other roads to China. For now, settle and breathe, and let the picture come: a story copied by hand, wrapped, carried on someone's back through cold passes, and read aloud somewhere new. Think of one story in your own life that someone else carried to you. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
Final nirvana. The passing the Buddha enters in the rest of the poem, carried on in Tibetan and Chinese after the Sanskrit breaks off, after his last journey and the relics shared. Today's word.
Your line: the poem traveled. Today, pass one good story on to someone who hasn't heard it, so it travels a little further. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: English translations of the full Buddhacarita follow the Sanskrit where it survives and the Tibetan or Chinese versions after that; the Buddha's relics are honored at stupas across Asia.

fork.setup: you're one of the kings. the Buddha has died, and every kingdom wants his relics. armies are gathering. what do you do?
options: give up your claim and go home.
fork.reveal: the kings nearly go to war, then agree to divide the relics, each carrying a portion home to honor.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old poem either survives or it doesn't.
what it means: this one survives in pieces: Sanskrit for the first part, Tibetan and Chinese for the whole.
what a scholar hears: readers of the later cantos work from translations, so they compare the Tibetan and Chinese to guess what the lost Sanskrit once said.

notes: Manuscript claim from the outline: the Sanskrit breaks off partway (in canto 14) and the full poem is preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations. Confirm; the script gives no canto numbers in speech. The source ref '18–28' assumes the 28-canto Tibetan/Chinese structure; confirm or drop the range.
Hook: 'long ago the poem was carried over the mountains and translated' gives no date; confirm it is fair as stated.

Confirm each episode appears in the later cantos: Anathapindika and the Jeta grove; the return to Kapilavastu; Devadatta and the elephant Nalagiri/Dhanapala; Amrapali's grove; the last journey and death between twin sala trees at Kushinagara; the dispute over the relics and their division.
Week look-back covers days 715–721 (Mara comes, Mara defeated, Perfect knowledge, The wheel turned, Many come, Mahakassapa comes, The rest of the poem).
Practice suggests a map route via Tibet and China; this is about the poem's translations, not a claim about a specific historical route.

Editor: removed the implied route India-mountains-Tibet-China (the Chinese version did not come through Tibet) from hook and practice; 'that's where the poem ends' softened since the last canto may go on past the relics; howItsDone drops 'usually' and 'at the heart of devotion'.

Audit: the surviving Sanskrit breaks off inside canto 14 (around 14.31), during the night of awakening itself, so the hook's 'stop not long after the night under the tree' was wrong; now 'in the middle of the night under the tree, before the dawn'. Confirm the verse number.
